newsitem.title: UK: Non-EMU states stuck with green money-EU official.
newsitem.headline: Non-EMU states stuck with green money-EU official.

text.p: Any EU countries which do not join in the European single currency are going to have to have some sort of agrimoney system, according to the EU official who runs the present system.

Jean Marc Gazagnes of the EU Commission's directorate general for agriculture told an audience in London on Wednesday that for countries which do not adopt the Euro, the system will basically remain the same as it is today.

It would not be possible simply to convert prices and amounts fixed in Euro into national currencies using the bank rate on the day of payment, Gazagnes, speaking to an Agra Europe conference on "Agrimoney and EMU," said.
"Such simplicity would be a dream come true, and all the more appealing since it would succeed decades of nightmarish agrimonetary complexity," Gazagnes said.
"But the reality is not so simple and it is wrong to raise false hopes in this regard."

The notion of an operative event would still have to be applied, he said. An example of an operative event would be the physical delivery to the customer in a case in which products are being bought or sold.
In the case of export refunds it would be the lodging of the customs declaration.
"Whatever the conversion rate fixed for agriculture, a minimum system would be needed to avoid serious disruptions in the common organisations of the markets," he said.

"It is not clear that a system as complicated as the one we have today will be needed," he said. But a system simply using a bank conversion rate of the day of an operative event would presuppose daily, often tiny, changes in the rates.
"Many traders already complain of the numerous changes that the current agrimonetary system produces, ie a maximum of four changes for a single member state in the first six months of 1996," he said.
But a monetary union covering France, Germany and the Benelux countries alone would cover nearly 50 per cent of the EU's agricultural production and practically 60 per cent of the trade.
Because the additional costs caused where currencies appreciate will be avoided, having these countries in a monetary union would mean a saving worth 500 million Ecu a year.
"Monetary Union is certainly a good thing for farmers, the food industry, trade and the budget," Gazagnes said. "This good thing will only get better as the Euro is adopted by more member states.

There are going to be some problems with the transition to the Euro, Gazagnes said. As things stand there are divergences between the common levels of institutional prices and direct aids set in Ecu and the levels expressed in national currencies.

The scale of the difficulties these divergences create will depend on how big they are. "The most appropriate solution for resolving the problems raised cannot, therefore be decided long before 1 January, 1999, Gazagnes said.
